youtube.baslik: Speechreading and Visual Cues | Lesson 264 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Which sounds can be seen on the lips, and which cannot? In this lesson we cover visemes, the limits of speechreading, how vision and hearing complement each other, audiovisual integration and the McGurk effect.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Tye-Murray, Foundations of Aural Rehabilitation: Children, Adults, and Their Family Members; Erber, Communication Therapy for Hearing-Impaired Adults; Sumby and Pollack, Visual contribution to speech intelligibility in noise, J Acoust Soc Am (1954); McGurk and MacDonald, Hearing lips and seeing voices, Nature (1976).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn what speechreading is, and which sounds can and cannot be seen on the lips.
We will also look at how vision and hearing combine in the brain and how this knowledge is used in the clinic.
Speechreading is trying to understand speech by watching the speaker's face and body.
Not only the lips are watched, but also the visible parts of the tongue and teeth, facial expression, head movements and gestures.
This is why the broader term speechreading is often preferred over lipreading, which focuses only on the lips.
People with normal hearing also look at the speaker's face in a noisy setting without noticing.
For a person with hearing loss, visual cues fill in an important part of the information hearing misses.
The parts that cannot be seen are guessed from the context of the topic and knowledge of the language.
A group of speech sounds that look the same on the lips is called a viseme.
For example, the lips close for all three sounds p, b and m; these three sounds look almost the same on the lips.
For f and v, the lower lip touches the upper teeth; this group is easy to see but cannot be told apart within itself.
In sounds such as t, d, n, s and z, the tongue works behind the teeth; the picture is unclear and the sounds blend together.
In the first sounds of shoe, chair and jam, the lips push forward; this helps tell them apart from other sounds.
Sounds made at the back of the mouth, such as k, g and h, are almost invisible on the lips.

notlar.metin: Together: p, b, m are separated

cumleler: Vision and hearing carry different features of speech, which is why they are so powerful together.
Where a sound is made, its place of articulation, is largely visible to the eye.
Whether a sound is voiced, and whether it comes through the nose, cannot be seen but is heard by the ear.
On this example audiogram, the low frequencies are preserved and there is a loss in the high frequencies.
This person misses place information in high-frequency consonants, but hears voicing and nasality in the low frequencies.
So the eye supplies the missing place, and the ear the voicing not visible on the lips; this is how p, b and m are separated.
Vowels are generally easier to follow on the lips than consonants.
For spread vowels the lips are stretched; for rounded vowels, as in boot and boat, the lips round and push forward.
The mouth opens more for open vowels and less for close vowels; this difference can also be followed by eye.
The difference between front and back vowels depends on where the tongue sits in the mouth and is hard to see on the lips.
As speech gets faster, lip shapes get shorter and blend together, so speaking rate matters for speechreading.

maddeler.metin: Pat, bat and mat look alike

cumleler: The biggest limit of speechreading is that many sounds are either invisible or look the same as other sounds.
So words such as pat, bat and mat, or mom, Bob and pop, look almost the same on the lips.
Words that look the same on the lips are called homophenes; they can only be told apart by context.
Speech is fast; the lip shape of a sound lasts a very short time and overlaps with neighboring sounds.
Speechreading for long periods requires intense attention and quickly tires the person.
The ability to understand speech from vision alone varies greatly from person to person.
So speechreading should be seen not as a stand-alone skill, but as a source that complements hearing.
The speaker's face must be clearly visible and speech should be at a natural pace; exaggerated lip movements distort the picture.
Light should fall on the speaker's face from the front; a person with a window behind them has a shadowed face.
The listener should be close to the speaker and face them; from the side many cues are lost.
The listener's visual acuity, attention and fatigue also determine success; checking glasses matters in older adults.
A known topic makes guessing easier, while an unexpected change of topic makes speechreading markedly harder.
A face mask blocks these cues completely; a clear mask or a written note can help in that case.
Chewing gum or putting a hand to the mouth while speaking also hides lip movements.
The brain combining auditory and visual speech information into a single percept is called audiovisual integration.

cumleler.yazi: In 1954, Sumby and Pollack measured how much seeing the speaker's face helps understanding in noise.
cumleler.ses: In nineteen fifty four, Sumby and Pollack measured how much seeing the speaker's face helps understanding in noise.

cumleler: In the graph, the gray curve shows understanding with hearing only, and the blue curve with the face also visible; this is an example.
The visual benefit was clearest in heavy noise, where understanding by hearing alone dropped.
So seeing the speaker's face in a noisy setting is especially valuable for a person with hearing loss.
In people with hearing loss too, understanding from both sources together is higher than from either one alone.
A famous example of how strongly vision and hearing combine is the McGurk effect.

cumleler.yazi: In 1976, McGurk and MacDonald played the syllable ba to the ear while showing a face saying ga on the screen.
cumleler.ses: In nineteen seventy six, McGurk and MacDonald played the syllable ba to the ear while showing a face saying ga on the screen.

cumleler: Most listeners said they heard neither ba nor ga, but da, a syllable in between.
Even when the person knows it is an illusion, the percept does not change; integration is automatic and fast.
This effect shows that the brain decodes speech by using hearing and vision together.
In the clinic, this can be used to explain that visual cues are not just an aid, but a natural part of perception.
In speechreading training, analytic exercises focus on recognizing visemes and lip shapes.
Synthetic exercises aim at understanding at the sentence and conversation level, using context.
Today most programs prefer exercises that use visual and auditory information together.
In most studies, gains in vision-only speechreading skill have remained limited.
Even so, training helps the person make a habit of looking at the speaker's face and adjusting the setting.
In group programs, speechreading practice is combined with communication strategies.

maddeler.metin: Video calls are easier than voice calls
A meeting seat facing the speakers

cumleler: In daily life, the first rule is that the speaker's face should be visible.
Video calls are easier for most people than voice-only phone calls because the face is visible; picture and sound must be in sync.
TV captions and speech-to-text apps strengthen visual support with text.
In health care settings, clear masks and giving important information in writing reduce breakdowns.
In a meeting, choosing a seat where the speakers' faces can be seen is also a simple but effective measure.
Seeing the teacher's face matters for children too; we will cover classroom seating in a later lesson.

sahneler.metin: Cover your mouth during live-voice speech testing; otherwise speechreading inflates the score. When explaining the results, turn your face to the patient.
cumleler: A clinical tip: when doing live-voice speech testing, cover your mouth so the patient cannot see it.
If the patient sees your lips, speechreading inflates the score and the result no longer reflects hearing alone.
When the test is over, do the opposite: face the patient while explaining the results and keep the light on your face.
That way the test stays valid, and the patient can use visual cues during counseling.

maddeler.metin: Eye carries place, ear carries voicing
Visual benefit is largest in noise

cumleler: Sounds that look the same on the lips form a viseme; p, b and m are an example.
Vision carries place of articulation, while hearing carries voicing and nasality; the two complement each other.
The benefit of seeing the speaker's face is clearest in noisy settings.
Speechreading has major limits, so it complements hearing rather than replacing it.

sahneler.soru: Which three sounds belong to the same viseme?
sahneler.aciklama: For p, b and m the lips _close_; they look the same on the lips.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: which of the following sounds belong to the same viseme group?

cumleler: The correct answer is A: p, b and m.
The lips close for all three; they can only be told apart by hearing or context.
